title: Exponents & Roots
coreInsight: Exponents encode repeated multiplicative structure, and roots reverse powers.
targetLearnerRealization: An exponent counts repeated factors, while a root asks for the base whose power produces a quantity.
learningObjectives: Interpret a^n as n factors of base a rather than a multiplied by n.
Keep the roles of base and exponent distinct.
Derive the same-base product rule by counting repeated factors.
Explain why exponents do not distribute over addition.
Interpret a square root as the nonnegative side length whose square gives an area.
Use zero exponents and structural comparison in a constrained exponent expression.

continuity.openingCallback: Compress repeated multiplication only after estimating whether the expanded product is reasonable.
closingSeeds: Prime factorizations can record repeated factors with exponents.
Power patterns can create repeating units digits.
Square roots connect square area back to side length.

misconceptionTargets.misconception: Taking a square root means dividing by 2.
The roles of base and exponent can be interchanged.

beats.purpose: Establish exponent notation as repeated multiplication by contrasting it with repeated addition and base-times-exponent.
beats.expectedRealization: 3^4 contains four factors of 3 and equals 81, not 12.
beats.transitionIn: Multiplication compresses repeated addition. Exponent notation compresses a different repetition: equal factors.
beats.whyNow: A direct expansion question surfaces the dominant exponent misconception before any exponent laws are introduced.
beats.entryBridge: Read the small raised number as a count of equal factors.
beats.exitBridge: The four belongs to the number of factor copies; the three is the factor being copied.
beats.reusedRepresentation: Base tiles repeated according to an exponent card.
learnerPrompts: Which number is copied, and how many factor copies are required?
beats.incorrectFeedback: The exponent counts factors of the base; it does not multiply the base once by the exponent.

visual.ariaLabel: Four copies of base three multiplied to make eighty-one

steps.title: Expand the notation
steps.body: The exponent 4 asks for four factors of the base 3.

resolution.takeaway: An exponent counts repeated factors, not repeated additions.

beats.purpose: Make base and exponent roles non-interchangeable through a numerical contrast.
beats.expectedRealization: Swapping base and exponent changes both the repeated factor and its number of copies.
beats.transitionIn: The base names the factor; the exponent counts its copies. Swap the roles and inspect what changes.

options.text: 2^5 = 32 and 5^2 = 25, so they are not equal.
Both equal 10 because base times exponent is unchanged.
Both equal 25 because the larger number controls the value.
Both equal 32 because exponent order never matters.

beats.correctFeedback: Yes. Five factors of 2 and two factors of 5 are different products.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Expand each power: count copies of its own base.

visual.ariaLabel: Expanded forms and values of two to the fifth and five squared

steps.title: Keep roles attached
steps.body: In 2^5, 2 is repeated five times. In 5^2, 5 is repeated twice. Swapping roles changes the structure.

resolution.takeaway: Base and exponent have different jobs and cannot generally be interchanged.

beats.purpose: Derive the same-base product rule from factor counting rather than memorization.
beats.expectedRealization: Multiplying powers with the same base joins their factor lists, so exponents add.
beats.transitionIn: Repeated-factor lists can be joined. Count the copies after multiplying two powers of the same base.
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. Three factors of 2 joined with two more make five factors of 2.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Expand both powers, then count the total number of factors equal to 2.

data.total: Same base: join factors, add exponents.

visual.ariaLabel: Three factors of two joined with two factors of two to make five factors

steps.title: Count rather than guess
steps.body: The product contains 3 + 2 = 5 copies of the same factor 2.

resolution.takeaway: For the same base, a^m × a^n = a^(m+n) because the factor counts join.

beats.purpose: Surface and repair false distribution of an exponent over addition.
beats.expectedRealization: A power applies to the complete parenthesized base; cross-products appear when expanded.
beats.transitionIn: The product rule joined factors with the same base. A sum inside parentheses is one complete base, not separate power targets.
beats.correctFeedback: Yes. The whole sum is the base and must be used as a factor twice.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Treat the parentheses as one base: square means multiply that complete base by itself.

steps.title: Locate the missing pieces
steps.body: Expanding gives 2·2 + 2·3 + 3·2 + 3·3. The expression 2^2 + 3^2 omits both cross-products.

resolution.takeaway: Exponents do not distribute over addition.

beats.purpose: Discover square root as reversing a square through a geometric side-length question.
beats.expectedRealization: The square root of an area is the nonnegative side length whose square produces it.
beats.transitionIn: Squaring uses two equal factors. Reverse that structure by hiding the factor and showing the product.
beats.prompt: A square has area 81 square units. What is its side length?
beats.incorrectFeedback: Find a nonnegative number that multiplies by itself to make 81; do not divide 81 by 2.

visual.ariaLabel: A square side length nine producing area eighty-one and the square root reversing it

steps.title: Reverse the equal factors
steps.body: Square area is side × side. Since 9 × 9 = 81, sqrt(81) = 9.

steps.title: Reject halving
steps.body: 81 ÷ 2 = 40.5 does not produce equal factors whose product is 81.

resolution.takeaway: The square root asks for the nonnegative number whose square is the given value.

beats.purpose: Derive the nonzero zero-exponent rule needed by the authentic transfer.
beats.expectedRealization: For nonzero a, a^0 must equal 1 to preserve quotient structure.
beats.transitionIn: Roots reverse powers. Division can also reveal what happens when a factor count falls to zero.
beats.prompt: The quotient 2^3 ÷ 2^3 equals 1. Cancelling three factors from three factors also leaves 2^(3-3) = 2^0. What must 2^0 equal?
beats.correctFeedback: Yes. A nonzero quantity divided by itself is 1, so 2^0 = 1.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Evaluate 2^3 ÷ 2^3 directly. The zero exponent must preserve that value.

steps.title: Count remaining factors
steps.body: Subtracting equal factor counts gives 2^(3-3) = 2^0, so 2^0 = 1.

resolution.takeaway: Every nonzero base raised to the zero power equals 1.

beats.purpose: Name powers, bases, exponents, and roots after their structures have been built and reversed.
beats.expectedRealization: Power and root notation compress and reverse repeated-factor structure.
beats.name: Powers and roots
beats.conciseDefinition: In a^n, a is the base and n is the exponent counting equal factors. A square root reverses squaring: sqrt(N) is the nonnegative number whose square is N.
beats.formalization: a^m · a^n = a^(m+n) for the same base · a^0 = 1 for a ≠ 0 · sqrt(a^2) = |a|
beats.memoryHook: Copy the base; count factors; root asks for the equal factor back.

beats.purpose: Apply base/exponent roles, zero powers, and structural comparison to optimize a constrained expression.
beats.expectedRealization: Placing zero in a nonzero exponent slot makes a neutral factor 1, leaving the other digits to form the larger of 3^2 and 2^3.
beats.transitionIn: The base and exponent cards now compete for four digit placements. The zero is especially sensitive to which role it receives.
beats.whyNow: The learner understands repeated factors and zero exponents, so the contest task can test structural placement instead of rote evaluation.
beats.entryBridge: Reject arrangements with zero as a base, then compare the surviving power structures with zero used as an exponent.
beats.exitBridge: The maximum 9 comes from a feasible arrangement, not from assuming a larger-looking exponent always wins.
beats.reusedRepresentation: Base cards with repeated factor copies controlled by exponent cards.
learnerPrompts: Which four slots must receive the digits 2, 0, 2, and 3?
What happens when zero is placed in a base?
Why is placing zero as an exponent useful, and which powers remain possible?
Which is larger, 3^2 or 2^3, and what arrangement attains it?
beats.incorrectFeedback: Put zero in an exponent so its nonzero base contributes 1, then compare the powers made from the remaining digits.

steps.title: Control the zero
steps.body: A zero base makes the whole product zero. A zero exponent on a nonzero base makes that factor 1.

steps.title: List the meaningful survivors
steps.body: With zero used as an exponent, the other power can be 3^2 = 9, 2^3 = 8, or 2^2 = 4.

resolution.takeaway: Compare what each base/exponent placement actually represents; visual size alone does not order powers.

beats.purpose: Assess exponent meaning through direct evaluation.
beats.whyNow: Return to a single power after the multi-slot contest expression.
beats.entryBridge: Use three copies of base 5, not 5 × 3.
learnerPrompts: How many factors of 5 does the exponent request?
beats.incorrectFeedback: Write three equal factors of 5 before evaluating.

resolution.takeaway: The exponent counts factors of the base.

beats.purpose: Assess square root as inverse of squaring.
beats.whyNow: Reverse a familiar perfect square directly.
beats.entryBridge: Search for the nonnegative equal factor whose product is 144.
beats.exitBridge: Squaring the result checks the root.
learnerPrompts: Which candidate multiplied by itself gives 144?
beats.incorrectFeedback: Test candidates by squaring; a square root is not half the number.

resolution.takeaway: Check a square root by squaring it.

beats.purpose: Assess same-base multiplication through factor counting.
beats.whyNow: Combine two compressed factor lists without expanding numerically too soon.
beats.entryBridge: Count all factors of 2 across both powers.
learnerPrompts: How many total copies of base 2 appear?
beats.incorrectFeedback: Join three factors of 2 with four more; do not multiply the exponents.

steps.title: Join factor lists
steps.body: Three copies plus four copies make seven copies: 2^3 × 2^4 = 2^7.

resolution.takeaway: Same-base products add factor counts, so their exponents add.

beats.purpose: Assess a power applied to a parenthesized sum and reject false distribution.
beats.whyNow: Change the base from one number to a complete expression.
beats.entryBridge: Evaluate or repeat the whole parenthesized base.
beats.exitBridge: The cross-products explain why separate squaring fails.
learnerPrompts: What complete quantity is used as the repeated factor?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. The base is 5, so its square is 25.
beats.incorrectFeedback: The exponent applies to the entire sum (3 + 2), not separately to each addend.

steps.title: Check the trap
steps.body: 3^2 + 2^2 = 13, which omits the two cross-products and is not equivalent.

resolution.takeaway: Powers do not distribute over addition.

beats.purpose: Assess reversing square area before computing a new geometric quantity.
beats.whyNow: Finish by using a root as an intermediate result rather than the final answer.
beats.entryBridge: Recover the side length from area, then answer the perimeter question.
beats.exitBridge: The final check reconnects side, area, and perimeter.
learnerPrompts: Which side length squares to 196, and what does perimeter require next?
beats.correctFeedback: Correct. The side is 14, so the perimeter is 56.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Find sqrt(196) first, then multiply that side length by 4.

steps.title: Compute and check
steps.body: The perimeter is 4(14) = 56, while the area remains 14^2 = 196.

resolution.takeaway: A root can recover a missing dimension before another calculation begins.

beats.purpose: Consolidate exponent structure, valid rules, roots, and verification.
beats.expectedRealization: Reliable power reasoning returns to factor structure rather than manipulating raised numbers visually.
beats.transitionIn: Repeated factors, sums, roots, zero exponents, and digit slots all used the same structural checks.
beats.prompt: Which actions belong in a reliable powers-and-roots routine? Select all four.

options.text: Identify the complete base and the exponent's factor count.
Expand a small example when checking what a rule really does.
Use exponent rules only when their base and operation conditions match.
Check a root by raising it back to the original power.

response.feedback: Each action protects a different structural meaning.

beats.correctFeedback: Yes—name roles, inspect factors, check rule conditions, and reverse roots to verify.
beats.incorrectFeedback: All four matter; exponent notation is compact, so factor structure and inverse checks keep it honest.

visual.ariaLabel: Four safeguards for working with powers and roots

steps.title: Return to meaning
steps.body: When a symbolic shortcut is uncertain, write the repeated factors or reverse the power. The structure decides which manipulation is valid.

resolution.takeaway: Build from factors; use rules with conditions; verify roots by powers.

beats.purpose: Connect exponent structure to mapped future number theory and geometry uses.
beats.expectedRealization: The same compressed factor counts support prime factorization, units-digit cycles, and geometric dimensions.
beats.transitionIn: A power records repeated copies of one factor, and a root recovers a repeated dimension. Those two ideas travel widely.
beats.prompt: How might exponent counts help compare prime factorizations, while repeating units digits help predict a huge power without evaluating it, and square roots recover side lengths from areas?
beats.takeaway: Powers compress multiplicative structure; roots and cycles let that structure be reversed or tracked.

notes: Design: multiplication's compression of repeated addition motivates powers as compression of repeated multiplication. Factor tiles separate base from exponent; a square-area reversal creates roots; a quotient derives the zero exponent needed by the authentic transfer. The closing connects the same structure to prime exponents, cycles, and geometry.

Beat outline: repeated-factor anchor -> base/exponent contrast -> derive same-base product -> addition trap -> square-root area -> derive zero exponent -> name powers and roots -> authentic digit-slot transfer -> five independent problems -> consolidation -> future-connection hook.

All generated answers were verified through factor expansions or inverse roots and independently by value audits, algebraic expansion, or geometric reconstruction. The lesson remains draft pending human review.
